questions.q: Why is security best described as a business enabler rather than just a cost?
keyPoints: It actively creates value, not just prevents loss
Builds the customer trust needed to attract and keep users
Ensures regulatory compliance so the business can operate
Differentiates the product and manages risk to protect revenue
questions.explanation: The naive view treats security as pure overhead; the mature view is that it enables the business to function and grow (hook: T-C-D-R — Trust, Compliance, Differentiation, Risk).

questions.q: Why is 'prevention is far cheaper than response' the core of justifying security spending?
keyPoints: A breach's cost includes large indirect costs (customer churn, reputation, lost revenue), not just fines and recovery
Prevention (training, code review, scanning) costs a small fraction of a breach
So preventing even one breach returns many times its cost
Prioritise spend with risk = likelihood x impact
questions.explanation: Quantifying both sides, and naming the indirect costs people forget, is what turns a vague answer into a 'justify' answer.

questions.q: Why is fixing a security flaw during design far cheaper than fixing it in production ('shift left')?
keyPoints: At design a flaw is just a decision to change before code depends on it
In production it needs emergency patches, downtime, re-testing, and possibly breach response
Textbook figure: a production fix costs ~63x a design-phase fix
So security-by-design builds protection into every SDLC phase rather than bolting it on
questions.explanation: Shift left = move security effort earlier on the timeline, where flaws are cheap to fix.

questions.q: What is the security-usability paradox, and why does it mean usability is a security requirement?
keyPoints: Adding more/harder security steps does not automatically make a system more secure
If security is too difficult, users circumvent it (sticky-note passwords, disabling MFA)
Those workarounds create new, often worse vulnerabilities
So a control users will bypass is no control at all
questions.explanation: The fix is 'secure default, easy right path' — make the safe option the default and the secure way the easiest way; treat bypasses as a design failure, not a user failure.

questions.q: Distinguish confidentiality from integrity, and explain why they fail independently.
keyPoints: Confidentiality = secrecy: who is allowed to READ the data
Integrity = accuracy: whether the data can be CHANGED by an unauthorised party
A spy who reads but changes nothing breaks confidentiality only
A vandal who scrambles a file they can't read breaks integrity only
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is protected by encryption and access control; integrity by hashing, digital signatures, and input validation.

questions.q: Distinguish authentication from authorisation, and state which comes first.
keyPoints: Authentication = verifying WHO you are (proving identity)
Authorisation = determining WHAT you are allowed to do
Authentication happens first, authorisation second
Being logged in (authenticated) does not mean being allowed (authorised)
questions.explanation: Example: logging into a school portal is authentication; being able to see your own grades but not change them or view others' is authorisation.

questions.q: Why are passwords hashed rather than encrypted?
keyPoints: Hashing is one-way (irreversible); encryption is two-way (reversible with a key)
You never need to recover a password — at login you only VERIFY a match
Because hashing is irreversible, a database breach doesn't reveal the passwords
Encryption needs a key that could also be stolen, making passwords recoverable
questions.explanation: Verification without recovery is exactly what a one-way function provides, so the recoverable form encryption gives is a liability you don't want.

questions.q: What roles do a salt and slow hashing play in secure password storage?
keyPoints: A salt is a unique random value added per user before hashing
It makes identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed rainbow tables
Slow hashing (bcrypt, Argon2, high-iteration PBKDF2) makes each guess expensive
This defeats brute force, which fast hashes like SHA-256 allow (billions of guesses/sec)
questions.explanation: The recipe is 'hash it, salt it, slow it' — and use an audited library rather than rolling your own.

questions.q: Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric encryption, and explain why HTTPS uses both.
keyPoints: Symmetric = one shared key (e.g. AES): fast, but has the key-sharing problem
Asymmetric = a public/private key pair (e.g. RSA): solves sharing, but slow
HTTPS uses hybrid encryption to get the best of both
Asymmetric is used once to agree a symmetric session key, then symmetric encrypts all traffic
questions.explanation: Asymmetric's public key can be shared openly, so it solves key distribution; symmetric's speed then handles the bulk data.

questions.q: How does a digital signature provide non-repudiation?
keyPoints: The sender hashes the document and encrypts that hash with their private key = the signature
The recipient re-hashes the document and decrypts the signature with the sender's public key
Matching hashes prove the document is unchanged (integrity) and authentic
Only the sender's private key could produce a signature their public key verifies, so they can't deny it
questions.explanation: Signing flips encryption's keys: sign with private, verify with public. Signing proves who and unchanged; it does not hide contents (that's encryption).

questions.q: How does sandboxing contribute to security by design?
keyPoints: It runs code in a restricted, isolated environment it cannot escape
Code is blocked from the file system, network, and other processes beyond what's permitted
It assumes code may be malicious or buggy and contains it from the outset
This enforces least privilege and limits the blast radius of any compromise
questions.explanation: Examples: browsers sandbox web-page JavaScript, mobile apps are walled off from each other, and analysts detonate malware in isolated VMs.

questions.q: Distinguish input validation from sanitisation, and explain why an allow-list beats a block-list.
keyPoints: Validation checks input against rules and REJECTS what doesn't conform
Sanitisation TRANSFORMS/escapes input so it's safe to use rather than rejecting it
An allow-list defines what's permitted; a block-list defines what's forbidden
Allow-list is preferred because defining what's good is finite while defining every bad input is impossible
questions.explanation: Attackers evade block-lists with encoding, mixed case, or new payloads; an allow-list rejects anything unexpected by default, including unknown attacks.

questions.q: How does a parameterised query prevent SQL injection?
keyPoints: SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a query and interpreted as code
A parameterised query uses placeholders and passes the data separately from the query text
The database compiles the query structure first, then treats the value as pure data
So input can never alter the command's structure — it's always treated as a literal value
questions.explanation: Injection and XSS are the same disease — input becoming code — just in different interpreters (database vs browser).

questions.q: How is privacy distinct from security, and why does data minimisation reduce risk?
keyPoints: Security protects data from unauthorised access; privacy governs whether you should collect it and how it's used
You can have perfect security and still violate privacy (e.g. secretly harvesting and selling data)
Data minimisation = collect less, keep less — only what's needed for the purpose
Data you never collect or have already deleted cannot be breached, misused, or stolen
questions.explanation: Minimisation directly shrinks the attack surface and the impact of any future breach; it's a security control, not just good manners.

questions.q: Why is 'the user is logged in' not enough to secure an API endpoint?
keyPoints: Authentication proves identity but does not grant permission for a specific resource
Without a per-request authorisation check, any logged-in user can access others' data
This is broken access control (insecure direct object reference) — e.g. changing an ID in the URL
Fix: on every request verify the caller owns the resource or holds a permitting role (least privilege)
questions.explanation: It's the most common real-world API breach — authenticated but not authorised.

questions.q: How can poor exception handling create a security vulnerability?
keyPoints: Returning a stack trace to the user leaks internals (file paths, library versions, DB structure) — information disclosure
A failed security check that lets execution continue can 'fail open', granting access it should deny
Fix: log full detail internally, return only a generic message externally
Always fail securely — default to denying the action on any error or doubt
questions.explanation: Log it private, show it generic, fail closed.

questions.q: Distinguish static (SAST) from dynamic (DAST) application security testing.
keyPoints: SAST analyses source code WITHOUT running it — 'Static = Source'
It finds flaws early and pinpoints the exact line, but produces false positives and misses runtime issues
DAST attacks the RUNNING app from outside like an attacker — 'Dynamic = Doing'
It finds genuinely exploitable and configuration flaws but runs late and can't pinpoint the code
questions.explanation: They're complementary: static finds it in the source early, dynamic proves it's exploitable at runtime — use both.

questions.q: Distinguish cross-site scripting (XSS) from cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
keyPoints: XSS injects a malicious script that runs in the victim's browser (the attacker runs code as you)
Root cause: untrusted input placed in a page without encoding; fix with output encoding + CSP
CSRF injects no script — it forges a request that rides the victim's already-authenticated session
Fix CSRF with an unpredictable anti-CSRF token plus SameSite cookies
questions.explanation: XSS injects a Script; CSRF rides a Session. Being logged in is exactly what CSRF exploits, so 'require login' does not stop it.

questions.q: How is a race condition (TOCTOU) exploited, and how is it prevented?
keyPoints: Correctness depends on the timing of concurrent operations
The attacker acts in the gap between a check and the dependent action (time-of-check to time-of-use)
Classic example: two simultaneous withdrawals both pass the balance check before either deducts — a double-spend
Fix: make the check and action atomic via a transaction with locking or an atomic conditional update
questions.explanation: Never assume single-threaded — a web server is always concurrent, handling many requests against the same data at once.

questions.q: Why does collaboration make software more secure, and why isn't it automatic?
keyPoints: Various points of view: a reviewer with different blind spots catches flaws the author couldn't see
Delegation by expertise: each security-critical part is handled by someone with real depth
Quality: combining diverse review and expertise yields fewer vulnerabilities and shares knowledge
Not automatic — the bystander effect and malicious insiders (e.g. the xz backdoor) mean it must be structured and trusted
questions.explanation: A solo developer can't reliably review their own code because the review carries the same blind spots as the writing.

questions.q: What makes a security metric useful rather than a vanity metric?
keyPoints: Useful metrics measure OUTCOMES that reflect whether you're genuinely safer, and drive a decision
Vanity metrics measure ACTIVITY that looks impressive but says nothing about real security
Good examples: mean time to detect/respond, vulnerability remediation time, patch coverage
Vanity examples: 'attacks blocked' or 'scans run' — mostly noise, no indication of safety
questions.explanation: Evaluation is a continuous loop — Measure, Audit (independently, against a standard like ISO 27001), Improve — because the threat landscape never stops changing.
